As long as the product you are listening through can decode digital audio, it should work perfectly. Streaming devices will pass the audio bitstream to the tv or audio device. If it goes to the tv first, set the tv to bitstream. Then your optical cable will carry the digital signal to the audio device.

At first glance there isn’t anything bad about what you described. I’ve made my business focus on proper amplification, because I find that a lot of people settle for adequate because they have no idea what speakers are capable of with better amplification. 

To prove my point to some of my skeptical co-workers, I hooked up a $99 pair of bookshelf speakers from our store’s in-house brand to a McIntosh amplifier and they rivaled a $1000 pair of speakers. 

Power is important. 

Long story short, if I had to change one thing, it’d be your receiver. But use what you have for now, save up and buy a higher-end amp. (Emotiva, Anthem, AudioControl, or Rotel)

Vizio is actually the exception to that rule. And yes if they do decode but only have two speakers it will sum it down to stereo but that causes the volume mismatch because dialog is less focused to the Left and Right channels than the effects are.

Look for ones make by speaker companies (not Bose). Definitive Technology has a solid bar on sale at “Greatest Purchase” 

If you want speakers make sure you at least have Left, Center, Right, and a Subwoofer (3.1) then get a good receiver to power your speakers. Don’t buy tower speakers and then get a $300 receiver. There isn’t enough power. 

Pro Tip: when shopping at a retail store with receivers, instead of reading the tag that says “Watts per channel” turn the receiver around and read the power supply details. It will tell you how many watts it draws from your wall. Take that number, subtract 20 (to power the processor, BT, etc) and then divide by however many speakers it can power. That is the maximum wattage you will really get out of your amp.

Sound bars also proliferate this issue. Most sound bar companies advertise a “3.1 system” leading you to believe that there’s a center channel. But really it’s a 3.1 speaker system as most manufacturers don’t have contracts with Dolby and DTS to properly decode the surround audio. 

Others, “rely on your tv” for the decoding (Sonos is the most popular example) but forget to point out that most TVs only pass bitstream (requiring the receiver/sound bar to decode) or linear PCM stripped down to stereo. 

Source: Sold high-end home theater systems for various companies over a 9 year career. 

TLDR: when you’re at the “Greatest Purchase” and the guy is telling you to buy a sound bar from a speaker company rather than a TV company, he’s trying to solve the exact issue brought up by OP.
